claims.text: The initial magnesium alloy exhibits unstable microstructures and elemental segregation.
Incomplete phase transformation causes poor oxidation resistance in the initial alloy.
Adding less than 2 at.% Mn or Fe enables transient-liquid-assisted densification at 850 °C.
The transient liquid facilitates rapid atomic diffusion.
Sintering at 850 °C with the additive suppresses magnesium volatility.
Transient-liquid-assisted sintering prevents segregated secondary phases.
A eutectic reaction between magnesium and 1.5 at.% manganese forms a transient liquid at 850 °C.
The transient liquid acts as a diffusion medium that homogenizes the matrix and eliminates segregation.
The transient liquid lowers the activation energy for mass transport.
Enhanced mass transport eliminates pores at 850 °C before significant magnesium evaporation occurs.
Rapid solidification during cooling traps manganese in a supersaturated magnesium solid solution.
The supersaturated solid solution inhibits nucleation of brittle intermetallic phases.
Sintering the modified alloy at 850 °C produces greater than 98% theoretical density.
The proposed process produces a single-phase-like microstructure with uniform elemental distribution.
The proposed microstructure has significantly improved oxidation and corrosion resistance relative to standard-sintered samples.
Standard solid-state sintering of the same alloy at 900 °C produces less than 95% relative density.
Standard sintering at 900 °C produces severe elemental segregation and unstable microstructures.
The poor baseline microstructure results from insufficient diffusion time and competing magnesium volatility.
Density fails below 800 °C because insufficient liquid forms.
Above 1000 °C, magnesium evaporation exceeds diffusion and causes volatility-driven porosity.
